questions.question: What is a store?
options: A place where only music plays
A place where buying and selling of things happen
questions.explanation: A store is a place where buying and selling of things happen. Stores buy products and then offer them to customers.

questions.question: What is all included in the price of a product in a store?
options: The item, transportation, storage, employees, and store operations
questions.explanation: The price of a product includes the costs of transportation, storage, store employees, and store operations.

questions.question: Chrumko walks past three different shops on his way home. Shop A has bright lights and friendly staff. Shop B is smaller and quieter. Shop C is far away but has lower prices. What is one reason why Shop A might charge higher prices than Shop C?
options: The products are always better quality
They spend more on lighting, decoration, and staff
There is no difference at all
questions.explanation: Different shops have different costs. Shop A's bright lights, decoration, and more staff are part of their operating costs, which may be reflected in higher prices.

questions.question: How does payment work in a store?
options: At checkout, products are scanned, each is added to the total price and you pay
questions.explanation: At checkout, products are scanned and the total amount appears on the display. This means a store works as an exchange of money for goods.

questions.question: What happens BEFORE a store sells products to customers?
options: The store buys products from manufacturers or suppliers
questions.explanation: Before selling to customers, stores must first buy products from manufacturers or suppliers. Then they arrange them on shelves.

questions.question: Chrumko buys bread for €2, milk for €1.50, and apples for €1. How much does he spend total?
questions.explanation: €2 + €1.50 + €1 = €4.50. Understanding how prices add up helps you manage your money at the store.

questions.question: Why might the same exact product cost different amounts in different stores?
options: Different stores have different rent, staff costs, and locations
The product is different quality in each store
questions.explanation: Different shops have different operating costs based on location, rent, employee wages, and overhead - all reflected in their prices.

questions.question: Chrumko goes to the shop with €10. He wants to buy juice (€2), bread (€2.50), and chocolate (€3). What is the problem?
options: There is no problem, he has enough money
The total is €7.50 but he only has €10... wait, he DOES have enough
He doesn't have enough money - the total would be €7.50 but he needs €10 for something else
questions.explanation: €2 + €2.50 + €3 = €7.50. Chrumko actually has enough! Always add up prices before buying to check your money.

questions.question: Why do stores need workers, heating, and lighting even when no customers are shopping?
options: To keep the store ready and attractive for when customers arrive
questions.explanation: Stores must maintain their premises constantly - heating keeps products fresh, lighting makes them visible, and workers organize everything. These are necessary costs.

questions.question: What is a discount?
options: A reduction in price from the original amount
questions.explanation: A discount means a product costs less than before. Stores use discounts to attract customers.

questions.question: Does a discount mean you must buy that item?
options: No, a lower price doesn't mean you need the item
questions.explanation: If someone buys something just because it's on sale, they may spend money on something they wouldn't have chosen otherwise.

questions.question: Chrumko goes to the shop to buy only a snack. He sees a discount on milk chocolate. What should he do?
options: Think about whether he really needs and wants it
questions.explanation: Chrumko realizes he didn't plan to buy candy and there's still some at home. He decides to keep his money.

questions.question: Is the discount good for Chrumko in this case?
options: No, it's not a good deal because Chrumko doesn't need it
questions.explanation: It's not a good deal for Chrumko because he doesn't need candy. A good discount is only for something you truly want and need.

questions.question: Which products SHOULD you buy even with a discount?
options: Things you want but don't need
Things you actually need and will use
Random items just because they're cheaper
questions.explanation: A discount is good when you need the item anyway. Discounts on things you don't need just waste money.

questions.question: A chocolate bar normally costs €3. It has a discount and now costs €2. How much do you save with the discount?
questions.explanation: €3 - €2 = €1 saved. But remember - this only matters if you actually need the chocolate!

questions.question: Compare: Buying something at full price that you really need vs. buying something at a discount that you don't need. Which is smarter?
options: The discounted item, because it's cheaper
The full-price item, because you actually need it
questions.explanation: The full-price item is smarter because you need it. Spending money on discounted things you don't need wastes money overall.

questions.question: There's a 50% discount on video games, but Chrumko's homework isn't finished. What's the wise choice?
options: Buy the game - the discount is too good to miss
Finish homework first, then think about the game later
Ask parents to buy it immediately
The discount forces him to buy
questions.explanation: A good discount doesn't change what's important right now. Homework comes first. Discounts will happen again in the future.

questions.question: Why do stores put big red discount signs in their windows?
options: To attract customers and make them want to shop there
questions.explanation: Stores use eye-catching signs because discounts attract customers. But remember: you only save money if you buy things you actually need.

questions.question: Why do stores use colorful signs and big letters?
options: To make products look more interesting and attract attention
questions.explanation: Stores use colorful signs and big letters to make products look more interesting and attract our attention.

questions.question: Chrumko sees a big yellow sign 'best value package at the best price'. What should he do?
options: Look at the actual price and compare with other products
questions.explanation: Chrumko should look at the actual price and compare with other products. A big sign doesn't automatically mean the best deal.

questions.question: Chrumko finds a product with a huge '30% OFF!' sign. But when he looks carefully, a similar product without the sign costs even less. What learned?
options: The sign always tells the truth
Marketing signs can be misleading - you must compare prices yourself
questions.explanation: Even with a discount sign, another product might be cheaper. Always compare, don't just trust the bright signs!

questions.question: What does Chrumko learn about shopping signs?
options: A big sign doesn't automatically mean the best deal
Always buy what has the biggest sign
questions.explanation: Chrumko learns that big signs are designed to catch your attention, not necessarily to show the best value. Compare before buying!

questions.question: Which is an example of a marketing trick used by stores?
options: Giving the lowest price to everyone
Placing colorful products at eye level and expensive items at top shelves
Telling customers not to come back
questions.explanation: Stores strategically place products where they're most visible and eye-catching to influence what you buy.

questions.question: A shop sign says '20% discount!' A pen originally costs €5. What's the sale price?
questions.explanation: 20% of €5 = €1. So €5 - €1 = €4. Understanding the math helps you spot real deals from fake ones.

questions.question: Compare two items: (A) Bright packaging, famous brand, high price with '25% OFF' sign. (B) Plain packaging, no brand, lower price, no discount. Which is likely better value?
options: Item A, because it has a discount sign
Item B, because it's actually cheaper after comparing real prices
questions.explanation: Item B is better value if it's actually cheaper. The sign and packaging don't determine real value - the actual price and what you get do.

questions.question: A new product has bright packaging and a celebrity's name on it. It costs twice as much as an unnamed product of the same quality. Should Chrumko buy it?
options: Yes, the celebrity makes it better
No, he's paying for packaging and the celebrity's name, not better quality
questions.explanation: Part of the high price is for marketing and celebrity endorsement, not necessarily for better quality. Smart shoppers look past the packaging.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of colorful, exciting marketing in stores?
options: To make shopping easier for customers
To make you WANT to buy, not necessarily what you NEED
questions.explanation: Marketing is designed to create desire and excitement, which can make you buy things you didn't plan for. Stay aware of this trick!

questions.question: What is an impulse purchase?
options: A quick purchase without planning or thinking
questions.explanation: An impulse purchase is a quick purchase without planning. It happens when something catches our interest and we decide immediately.

questions.question: Where do impulse purchases often happen?
options: At the checkout, where small items are easily visible
questions.explanation: Impulse purchases often happen at checkout, where small items are easily visible and we get tempted by them.

questions.question: Chrumko stands at checkout with his mom. He sees colorful gum right by the till. What happens?
options: He gets tempted to buy it
questions.explanation: Chrumko gets tempted to buy the gum. It's placed exactly where everyone notices it, and there's a lot of temptation.

questions.question: What should Chrumko do when he wants something at the checkout?
options: Wait a moment and think about whether he really needs it
questions.explanation: Chrumko realizes he still has sweets from yesterday at home. He waits and doesn't buy the gum. The urge passes quickly.

questions.question: What's the best way to resist impulse buying at the checkout?
options: Pause for 30 seconds and ask: do I really need this?
questions.explanation: A 30-second pause usually stops the urge to impulse buy. Most cravings pass quickly if you wait.

questions.question: Chrumko impulse buys a candy bar for €2 every time he goes shopping (2 times per week). How much does he waste per month on impulse buys?
questions.explanation: 2 times per week × €2 = €4/week. €4 × 4 weeks = €16/month. Small impulse purchases add up quickly!

questions.question: Compare: Buying one candy at checkout vs. buying candy you planned for at home. Which wastes less money?
options: Planned purchase at home - you avoid checkout temptation
questions.explanation: Planned purchases at home are smarter because you avoid the impulse-triggering environment of the checkout.

questions.question: Chrumko is at the shop feeling bored. He hasn't planned to buy candy, but sees some. What is happening?
options: He needs the candy for nutrition
Boredom is making him want to buy something to feel better (emotional shopping)
questions.explanation: When we're bored or sad, we sometimes buy things to feel better. This is emotional impulse buying - recognizing it helps you resist.

questions.question: Why do stores put small, tempting items at the checkout?
options: To help customers remember what they forgot
Because people are most tempted to impulse buy while waiting in line
These items don't sell well anywhere else
questions.explanation: Checkout placement is strategic - stores know you're waiting, can see the items, and might impulse buy. It's designed to increase sales.

lessons.lessonName: How to Make Your Own Decisions

questions.question: How can you tell if you want something because you need it?
options: Ask yourself: do I need it? Will I use it for a long time?
questions.explanation: It helps to ask yourself: Do I need it? Will I use it for a long time? Is it worth spending money on?

questions.question: Chrumko goes to buy a notebook. He sees a pen with a colorful package. What should he do?
options: Stop and think about whether he really needs it
questions.explanation: Chrumko should stop and think about whether he really needs the pen.

questions.question: What does Chrumko find out about the pen at home?
options: He already has two working pens at home
questions.explanation: Chrumko remembers he still has two working pens at home and doesn't really need a new one.

questions.question: What does Chrumko finally decide?
options: Buy both the pen and notebook
Buy only the notebook and leave the pen in the store
questions.explanation: Chrumko buys only the notebook and leaves the pen in the store. A few days later he's glad he spent money only on what he needed.

questions.question: Which question helps you make smart buying decisions?
options: Will I actually use this regularly?
Is it the most expensive option?
questions.explanation: Asking if you'll actually use something regularly helps you buy things that provide real value.

questions.question: Chrumko has €20. He needs a pen (€2), notebook (€5), and pencils (€3). He sees sneakers he wants (€15). How much would he have left after the essentials?
questions.explanation: €2 + €5 + €3 = €10 needed. €20 - €10 = €10 left. Not enough for €15 sneakers. Good decisions require looking at the math!

questions.question: Compare: (A) Buying a cheap item you don't really need vs. (B) Buying nothing and keeping your money. Which is smarter?
options: A, because something is better than nothing
B, because you keep money for things you actually need
questions.explanation: Keeping money for real needs is smarter than spending on things you don't need, even if they're cheap.

questions.question: Your friend has a toy you think is cool. You feel pressure to buy the same one. What should you think?
options: You must buy it to be cool too
Your friend likes it, but does it fit YOUR needs and budget?
Everyone has to have the same things
Friends force you to buy things
questions.explanation: What your friend likes might not be right for you. Make your own decisions based on your needs, not peer pressure.

questions.question: What is the first step in making a smart buying decision?
options: Ask: Do I really need this, or do I just want it?
questions.explanation: The first question is whether you need it. If yes, then check price. If no, keep your money. Your own judgment matters most!
